title: Mean, median and outliers
content: The mean is the sum of the observations divided by their count. The median is the middle value after sorting; for an even count, average the two middle values. For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the mean is 6 and the median is 3. The outlier 18 pulls the mean upwards. The median is often a better description of a typical value in a strongly skewed distribution.

title: Population and sample variance
content: Variance measures squared distances from the mean. Population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by N. Sample variance uses n-1 when estimating a population variance from a sample. For 2, 4, 6, the mean is 4 and the squared deviations sum to 8. Population variance is 8/3; sample variance is 4. Standard deviation is the square root of variance, so the sample standard deviation is 2. Decide whether the data describe the entire population or a sample before choosing the denominator.

title: Conditional probability and independence
content: Conditional probability P(A|B) equals P(A and B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0. Events are independent when knowing B does not change the probability of A. For a fair die, let A be an even result and B a result greater than 3. P(A)=1/2, but P(A|B)=2/3 because 4 and 6 are even among 4, 5, 6. These events are not independent. Independent fair coin tosses provide a contrasting example: the next toss still has probability 1/2 of heads after a head.

title: Interpreting confidence intervals
content: A frequentist 95% confidence-interval procedure covers the fixed population parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. It does not assign a 95% probability to the fixed parameter lying in one particular observed interval. A larger random sample usually gives a narrower interval when other conditions are comparable. Report the estimate, interval, sample size and assumptions. A confidence interval does not repair bias from an unrepresentative sample.

title: Correlation and causation
content: Correlation describes association between variables, not a causal effect. Ice-cream sales and swimming incidents may both rise in hot weather: temperature is a possible confounder. A scatterplot helps reveal patterns, unusual observations and nonlinear relationships. Randomised experiments can strengthen causal evidence when properly designed; an observational correlation alone does not establish causation.

title: Practice task — synthetic course policy
content: This is a fictional demonstration module, STAT-DEMO. The practice assignment asks students to summarise a small dataset, justify a measure of centre, calculate sample variance and explain one limitation. The demonstration rubric allocates 40% to correct calculations, 40% to interpretation and 20% to clear communication. No real deadline or university submission policy is specified.
